strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis: Formal treatment of reward noise in GRPO/Dr.GRPO with clear convergence guarantees (Theorems 4.1-4.2) showing noise leads to strictly worse fixed points

Novel insight on variance normalization: Shows that linear reward correction alone is insufficient due to GRPO's standardization invariance; the solution requiring both mean and variance correction (Mk(q)) is non-obvious and well-motivated

Comprehensive theoretical results: Policy improvement bounds with explicit sample complexity for noise estimation (Proposition 5.6), gradient analysis quantifying shrinkage factor (Theorem 5.4), and monotonic improvement guarantees

Strong synthetic experiments: Two-stage protocol validates theory under perfect assumptions (controlled flip rates) before testing on realistic noisy reward models; controlled setting shows method sometimes exceeds noiseless baseline
Consistent improvements on math tasks: 6.7pp gain on GSM8K and 4+ pp on MATH across models demonstrates practical utility in domain with verifiable ground truth
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-structured mathematical exposition with complete proofs in appendix, fixed random seeds, detailed hyperparameters, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited theoretical scope: Restriction to binary rewards with query-independent constant flip rates (ρ⁺, ρ⁻) is significant; real errors likely depend on query difficulty. Assumption 1-ρ⁺-ρ⁻ > 0 is necessary but limiting

Inconsistent empirical gains: Code generation improvements are modest (1.5pp), and method degrades severely on highly noisy models (RM-Mistral-7B with ρ⁺=0.53 shows only 1.49pp gain), limiting practical utility for noisiest scenarios

Noise estimation procedure: Requires artificially corrupting 50% of answers for balanced calibration—assumes this mimics real reward model errors well. Calibration relative error of ~23% is substantial and could propagate through correction

Insufficient baseline comparisons: Only compares to uncorrected GRPO/Dr.GRPO; lacks comparison to alternative robustness approaches (ensemble reward models, regularized reward learning, contrastive methods mentioned in related work)
Limited experimental scale: Models are small (0.6B-1B primarily; max 4B), only two domains tested (math, code), and unclear how method scales to frontier models (13B+) or other RLVR tasks

Numerical stability concerns: Variance estimator (Proposition 5.3) subtracts noise-induced variance components and requires clipping to handle negatives; effect on unbiased property under clipping not analyzed. Flip rate estimation error propagates as scaling factor M'k(q) but empirical impact not measured
No statistical significance testing: Results reported as single runs without error bars or confidence intervals across runs; synthetic improvements could have large variance

Insufficient analysis of failure modes: When noise becomes extreme or flip rates poorly estimated, method effectiveness degrades significantly, but paper provides limited guidance on applicability boundaries

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis: Formal characterization of how Bernoulli reward noise attenuates the GRPO learning signal by factor (1-ρ⁺-ρ⁻), with proof of convergence to worse fixed points (Corollary 4.3) and explicit sample complexity bounds (Proposition 5.6)

Well-motivated problem: Addresses genuinely important and underexplored interaction between reward noise and group-based policy optimization in RLVR, with concrete examples of noise sources (false positives from LLM judges, false negatives from parsers)

Principled methodological approach: Clever insight that GRPO's standardization invariance defeats linear Natarajan correction, requiring variance-adjusted normalization (Mk(q)) - demonstrates thoughtful technical problem-solving
Strong experimental design: Two-stage validation (synthetic noise with known rates → realistic reward models with estimated rates) effectively separates theory verification from practical evaluation

Clear presentation and reproducibility: Algorithm 1 is concrete, comprehensive proofs provided, code made available, hyperparameters and experimental details well-documented, limitations honestly discussed
Novel connection: First formal analysis connecting label-noise correction from supervised learning to policy gradient methods, opening new research direction
weaknesses: Limited empirical improvements on realistic reward models: Math tasks show 6.7% maximum improvement (52.52%→59.21%), code tasks only 1.5% (8.55%→8.68%). Large gap between impressive synthetic results (Table 1-2) and modest real-world gains raises practical utility questions; no statistical significance testing reported

Noise estimation procedure has practical limitations: Requires 20% held-out samples artificially corrupted by modifying numbers/adding bugs—may not reflect actual failure modes. Proposition 5.6 shows ~23.5% relative error bounds; paper doesn't analyze error propagation into performance or when estimation fails

Restrictive modeling assumptions: Binary rewards only (continuous scores must be thresholded, losing information); class-conditional Bernoulli noise may oversimplify error patterns; global flip rates (acknowledged but significant limitation since difficulty/topic likely affect noise rates); assumes 1-ρ⁺-ρ⁻>0

Limited experimental scope: Only 0.6B and 1B models as primary focus; no 7B+ models (more practically relevant); only 10 training epochs; only two domains (math/code); notably, no comparison to competing noise-robust methods (ensembles, Yan et al. 2024, Bukharin et al. 2024)

Synthetic noise results show regularization confound: Table 1 shows corrections sometimes exceed noiseless baseline (60.11%→70.55%), suggesting noise correction acts as implicit regularization. Paper acknowledges but doesn't thoroughly investigate, leaving ambiguity about whether gains are from denoising or regularization

Incomplete ablation studies: No sensitivity analysis for clipping threshold ε; no convergence speed comparison; no sensitivity to β; limited study of how results degrade with estimation errors (Theorem 5.5 characterized but not empirically validated); concerning minimal improvements on extremely noisy RM-Mistral-7B (53% FPR)

Theory-practice gap on noise estimation: Theorems assume known flip rates; practical impact of estimation errors (Theorem 5.5's scaling factor) not empirically studied; no guidance on detecting failed estimation or determining when 20% holdout suffices
Presentation issues: Dense notation in places; Figure 1 could better explain practical significance; missing guidance on when practitioners should use this method vs alternatives
